titulo.texto: Peoples of Corn and Stone, and the Olmec Phenomenon

frase_gancho.texto: Figurines, vessels and a catfish-shaped incense burner: this is how village life begins in Morelos more than three thousand years ago.

puente_narrativo.texto: Continue through the palace: go up to the terrace where the cuexcomate is.

guion_corto.texto: About three thousand five hundred years ago, the communities of Morelos were already living from growing corn. The Peoples of Corn and Stone hall shows female figurines, bottles and cooking pots dated between fifteen hundred and twelve hundred before the Common Era. They are everyday objects, not luxury ones. In the next hall, The Olmec Phenomenon, something else appears: the influence of a Gulf Coast culture on the pottery and sculpture of Morelos. Among the pieces are the Oaxtepec vessel and a catfish-shaped incense burner. There is also a replica of Monument thirty-six from Chalcatzingo, a site in Morelos with stone reliefs. Here the museum talks about villages, not kings.

guion_largo.texto:
These two halls tell one story in two tones. The first is about everyday life; the second, about the ideas that traveled.

In Peoples of Corn and Stone, the museum gathers objects from communities that lived in Morelos between fifteen hundred and twelve hundred before the Common Era. There are female clay figurines, bottles and cooking pots. Figurines are among the most common objects of that era in Mesoamerica. What they were for is still debated. Some specialists link them to fertility or to household rituals. The pots and bottles are easier to read. They were for cooking, storing and serving.

The hall’s title speaks of corn and stone for a reason. Corn was the basis of food and of life for the Mesoamerican peoples. Stone was the material for tools and, later, for sculptures and temples. Between the two, a stable way of life takes shape.

The second hall is called The Olmec Phenomenon. The Olmec were a Gulf Coast culture, from the shores of the Gulf of Mexico, famous for their colossal heads. Their influence reached many regions, including Morelos. In the hall there is pottery and sculpture from Morelos that show features of that style.

Among the most important pieces is the Oaxtepec vessel. Another is a catfish-shaped incense burner, that is, one shaped like a whiskered river fish. And there is a replica of Monument thirty-six from Chalcatzingo. Chalcatzingo is an archaeological site in Morelos with reliefs carved into the rocks of a hill. When a museum shows a replica, it is because the original stayed in its place.

The word influence is important. Specialists debate how the Olmec style reached Morelos: whether through trade, through people traveling or through an exchange of ideas. What you can see in the display cases is that the local communities made their own version.

The museum points to Xochicalco as the most important archaeological site among those it presents. Xochicalco is an ancient city of Morelos, built on a hill and much later than the villages of this hall. The two eras live side by side in the museum and show how long the thread of the state’s history is.

One way of looking at the two halls together is to ask what changes and what stays. The objects and the styles change. What stays is clay, corn and the need to store, cook and share.

The tour through these halls leaves a question worth taking to the rest of the museum. In the year fifteen hundred before the Common Era there were already villages with pots, figurines and shared styles. So what came before the tecpan, the Tlahuica plaza and the Palace of Cortés? Much more history than is usually told. If you have time left, look again at a vessel or a figurine and think about the hands that made it. Each piece was made by a person, for a specific use.

texto: Find the Oaxtepec vessel and the catfish-shaped incense burner and compare them: which looks like everyday use and which like ceremony?
Find the female figurines and notice how the artist handled the face and the body
Look at the replica of Monument thirty-six from Chalcatzingo and think about why a copy is displayed

texto.Pieces: Oaxtepec vessel, catfish-shaped incense burner and replica of Monument 36 from Chalcatzingo

texto.pregunta: Myth: The Olmec were the founders of all the cultures of Mesoamerica.
texto.respuesta: Reality: Specialists debate how much they influenced others. In Morelos their influence can be seen, but the local communities made their own style.
